title: Poetry: The Art of Foregrounding
description: Master Poetic Licence, Parallelism, and the 5 levels of linguistic Deviation.

lessons.title: Poetic Licence & Language Levels
lessons.subtitle: How poets break the rules and the structure of language.

content.heading: Theoretical: Poetic Licence
content.body: Poetic Licence is the poet's right to ignore rules and conventions generally observed by users of the language. This allows for artistic creativity and the bending of grammatical, phonological, or lexical norms.

content.heading: Theoretical: Levels of Language
content.body:
Language is structured in 3 levels: 
1. Realization: Sounds (Phonology) and Marks (Graphology).
2. Form: Words (Lexicon) and Grammar (Syntax).
3. Meaning: Semantics (Literal) and Pragmatics (Contextual).

content.heading: Theoretical: Foregrounding
content.body: Refers to the ways in which certain aspects of a text are made to stand out or appear prominent (Prominence). The three main methods are Parallelism, Deviation, and Repetition.

lessons.title: The 5 Levels of Deviation
lessons.subtitle: Diving deep into how language is bent.

content.heading: Theoretical: Deviation
content.body: Extra irregularity. Deviation works by disrupting or departing either from readersâ€™ expectations or from a pattern established by the text. This is essentially a division between external deviation and internal deviation.

content.heading: Applied: Types of Deviation
content.body: Breaking language at every level:

steps.label: Lexical
steps.body: Creating new words (Neologism) via Affixation (foresuffer), Compounding (widow-making), or Functional Conversion (using verb as noun).

steps.label: Syntactic
steps.body: Breaking grammar rules like Inversion ('Then spake King Arthur').

steps.label: Phonological
steps.body: Breaking sound rules like Elision ('t'assault') or Syncope ('o'er').

steps.label: Graphological
steps.body: Visual deviation like splitting words vertically or using odd capitalization.

steps.label: Semantic
steps.body: Breaking logic via Metaphor or Paradox (e.g., 'Death feeds on his mute voice').

title: Cohesion: The Glue of Texts
description: Learn how reference, ellipsis, conjunctions, and lexical choices tie sentences together.

lessons.title: Reference Cohesion
lessons.subtitle: Anaphoric and Cataphoric pointers.

content.heading: Theoretical: Cohesion
content.body: The linguistic means by which sentences are woven together to make texts. It refers to all the linguistic ways in which words across sentences link up.

content.heading: Theoretical: Reference Types
content.body:
1. Anaphoric: Referring BACK to something already mentioned (e.g., 'Mary arrived. **She** was tired').
2. Cataphoric: Referring FORWARD to something yet to be mentioned (e.g., 'When **he** arrived, John slept').

lessons.title: Ellipsis (Nominal, Verbal, Clausal)
lessons.subtitle: The art of omitting unnecessary repetition.

content.heading: Theoretical: Ellipsis
content.body: Material is left out since its repetition or near-repetition is felt to be unnecessary.

content.heading: Applied: The 3 Types of Ellipsis
content.body: Identifying what was deleted:

steps.label: Nominal Ellipsis
steps.body: The **Noun** is omitted. Example: 'I saw two pens. I bought **both** [pens].'

steps.label: Verbal Ellipsis
steps.body: The **Verb** is omitted. Example: 'Have you been swimming?' 'Yes, I **have** [been swimming].'

steps.label: Clausal Ellipsis
steps.body: An entire **Clause** is omitted. Example: 'Why didn't you go?' 'I don't **know** [why I didn't go].'

lessons.title: Conjunctions & Lexical Cohesion
lessons.subtitle: Signposting and word patterns.

content.heading: Theoretical: Conjunction Cohesion
content.body: Use of words/phrases to clarify the semantic or logical relationship. The 4 types are: Additive, Adversative, Causal, and Temporal.

content.heading: Theoretical: Lexical Cohesion
content.body:
Integratedness created via content words. Main types include:
1. Repetition: Reusing the same word.
2. Synonymy: Using similar words.
3. Hyponymy: Using category relationships (e.g., rose is a hyponym of flower).
4. Collocation: Words that commonly occur together (e.g., strong tea).

title: Modality: Opinion & Attitude
description: Understanding how speakers qualify their claims and use evaluative devices.

lessons.title: The 4 Modality Parameters
lessons.subtitle: Probability, Obligation, Willingness, and Usuality.

content.heading: Theoretical: Modality
content.body: The cover term for the ways available to a speaker within a language for expressing 'opinion or attitude'. It denotes linguistic means for qualifying any claim.

content.heading: Applied: Modality Parameters
content.body: How we qualify language:

steps.label: Probability
steps.body: Likelihood (might, may, must, certainly).

steps.label: Obligation
steps.body: Necessity (should, ought to, must).

steps.label: Willingness
steps.body: Readiness/Desire (will, would, willing).

steps.label: Usuality
steps.body: Frequency (always, usually, rarely).

lessons.title: Evaluative Devices & Generic Sentences
lessons.subtitle: How stance is revealed through timeless truths.

content.heading: Theoretical: Evaluative Devices
content.body: Means by which a speaker's stance is revealed. Includes Evaluative Verbs (regret), Adjectives (admirable), and Generic Sentences.

content.heading: Theoretical: Generic Sentences
content.body: Sentences which assert something to be a general truth, typically timelessly true. Usually in the simple present tense (e.g., 'Afghanistan is the land of Pashtuns').

title: Narrative Structure (Labov)
description: Analyzing the 6 essential parts of any well-formed story.

lessons.title: Labov's 6-Part Schema
lessons.subtitle: The skeleton of every narrative.

content.heading: Theoretical: Labov's Model
content.body:
1. **Abstract**: Summary of the story.
2. **Orientation**: Who, when, where.
3. **Complicating Action**: Main events.
4. **Evaluation**: Why the story is worth telling.
5. **Resolution**: How it ends.
6. **Coda**: Returns the listener to the present.

content.heading: Applied: Evaluation Types
content.body: Evaluation is the soul of the narrative. It includes:

steps.label: Intensifying
steps.body: Vividness via gestures, repetitions, or dramatic sounds.

steps.label: Comparator
steps.body: Alternative narrative developments (negative/modal sentences).

steps.label: Correlative
steps.body: Secondary activities contemporaneous with events.

steps.label: Explicative
steps.body: Giving background reasons and causes.

title: Discourse Structure (Birmingham)
description: Treating conversation as a rule-governed system.

lessons.title: Hierarchical System & Moves
lessons.subtitle: Opening, Supporting, and Challenging moves.

content.heading: Theoretical: Birmingham Model
content.body: Treats conversation as a Rule-governed or Hierarchical system where moves are the key interactive units.

content.heading: Applied: Discourse Moves
content.body: How we interact:

steps.label: Opening Move
steps.body: Essential topic-carrying items which are recognisably 'new'.

steps.label: Supporting Move
steps.body: Occurring after any other type of move and involving items that concur.

steps.label: Challenging Move
steps.body: Functioning to hold up the progress of a topic.

title: Grice's Maxims & Implicature
description: Conversational cooperation and the art of hidden meaning.

lessons.title: The 4 Conversational Maxims
lessons.subtitle: Quality, Quantity, Relation, and Manner.

content.heading: Theoretical: The Cooperative Principle
content.body: The CP is a basic assumption that speakers normally intend to accomplish purposeful and effective communication.

content.heading: Applied: The 4 Maxims
content.body: The 4 rules of talk:

steps.label: Quality
steps.body: Be truthful (Don't say things that are false).

steps.label: Quantity
steps.body: Be as informative as required (Not too much or too little).

steps.label: Relation
steps.body: Be relevant (Say things that are relevant in context).

steps.label: Manner
steps.body: Be clear (Avoid obscurity and ambiguity).

title: Politeness & Face
description: Understanding social dynamics and face-threatening acts.

lessons.title: Face & Politeness Strategies
lessons.subtitle: Appreciation vs. Freedom.

content.heading: Theoretical: Positive & Negative Face
content.body:
1. **Positive Face**: Wish to be liked and approved of by others.
2. **Negative Face**: Wish not to be coerced or forced; desire for freedom from imposition.

content.heading: Applied: Politeness Strategies
content.body: Identify the strategy:

steps.label: Positive Politeness
steps.body: 'What a fantastic garden you have.' (Compliment/Solidarity).

steps.label: Negative Politeness
steps.body: 'Could you find me a computer so I can check my e-mail?' (Hedged request).

steps.label: Negative Politeness
steps.body: 'I don't suppose you could give us a lift.' (Being pessimistic).

steps.label: Off-record
steps.body: Dropping a hint (e.g., 'Our vacuum cleaner just broke down').

steps.label: Bald on-record
steps.body: Direct command without redress (e.g., 'Open the window').

title: Practical Exam Prep
description: Model answers and cheat sheets for the final exam.

lessons.title: Final Review & Cheat Sheets
lessons.subtitle: The essential list for exam night.

content.heading: Theoretical: Key Exam Triggers
content.body:
1. Semantic deviation -> Metaphor or Paradox.
2. Lexical Cohesion -> Reiteration, Synonymy, Hyponymy, Collocation.
3. Conjunctions -> Additive, Adversative, Causal, Temporal.

content.heading: Applied: Exam Strategy
content.body: How to tackle the paper:

steps.label: Definitions
steps.body: Memorize exact phrasing for 'Generic Sentence', 'Face', and 'Modality'.

steps.label: Maxims
steps.body: Always state both the Flouted Maxim and the Implicature.

steps.label: True/False
steps.body: Correct the false ones! (e.g., Pessimism is NOT Positive Politeness).
